tldr: JEPA-style world models plan without reward functions, scoring actions using distances in a frozen latent space alone. This work demonstrates that they barely rank candidate actions correctly in practice, and reveals that the only reason tasks appeared solved was that frequent step-by-step closed-loop replanning (MPC) was masking the errors.
hero_caption: Action ranking evaluation results on official released JEPA-WM checkpoints. In Push-T, 96.8% of anchors select a suboptimal candidate as top-1, and in MetaWorld reach-wall, 100% do (left). The gap between the chosen action's cost and the true optimum (regret) is also substantial (right).
overview:
Recently, reward-free latent world models (such as JEPA-WM and DINO-WM) have attracted significant attention. Instead of learning value or reward functions, they plan simply by using closeness to a goal embedding in a frozen, self-supervised latent space as their scoring metric. This approach relies entirely on the assumption that latent closeness is action-rankable: candidate actions with smaller latent distances should have lower true task costs. Surprisingly, however, no prior benchmark had directly audited whether this assumption actually holds in official released models.

To fill this gap, the authors introduce ARC-Bench, a no-leak fixed-candidate audit protocol, and rigorously evaluate official released checkpoints. The findings are striking. In manipulation tasks (Push-T and MetaWorld), the candidate ranked first by the model is suboptimal 96.8% to 100% of the time. In maze domains, the model frequently selects opposite-direction actions with high confidence—a failure mode termed a "Mirage." Furthermore, replacing the visual backbone with video-pretrained encoders like V-JEPA 1 or V-JEPA 2 does not resolve this geometric defect.

Why did prior studies report high success rates despite such broken evaluation capabilities? The trick lies in closed-loop replanning. Under step-by-step replanning ($k=1$), taking a bad action at one step is immediately overwritten by fresh observations at the next step, resetting the latent state before errors can compound. When the authors widened the replanning interval to 6 steps ($k=6$) to force open-loop execution, success rates collapsed dramatically: from 89.6% down to 61.8% in PointMaze, and from 36.1% down to 12.5% in Push-T. High closed-loop success rates did not indicate good representations; they merely showed that an aggressive error-correcting control loop was desperately masking underlying defects.
contributions: Constructed ARC-Bench, a no-leak fixed-candidate evaluation benchmark designed to directly measure the action-ranking capability of frozen JEPA-style world models.
Demonstrated that in official released JEPA-WM checkpoints, 96.8% to 100% of top-scored candidate actions are suboptimal, proving that severe ranking failures (Mirages) occur structurally.
Showed that switching backbones to video-pretrained models (V-JEPA 1/2) or scaling up candidate sampling budgets does not repair the ranking breakdown itself.

Identified the masking mechanism behind high closed-loop success rates: errors are continually overwritten by step-by-step replanning, and reducing replanning frequency leads to a dramatic collapse in task success.

sections.heading: Can We Trust Latent Closeness?: Auditing an Overlooked Core Assumption
sections.summary: Reward-free planning via latent distance relies on the unverified assumption that latent distance reflects task progress. This paper rigorously audits this assumption, shows that it fails completely in official checkpoints, and reveals why that failure went unnoticed.
sections.details:
Reward-free latent world models, such as DINO-WM and JEPA-WM, avoid training reinforcement learning value functions. Instead, they roll out future latent states using self-supervised encoders and predictive models, choosing the candidate action that lands closest in Euclidean distance to the goal embedding. This approach eliminates the hassle of reward engineering, but it rests on a massive assumption: that latent closeness is action-rankable, meaning ordering candidates by latent distance agrees with ordering them by true task cost.

What happens when this assumption breaks? The model confidently picks a candidate as top-1 that appears extremely close in latent space, even though executing it actually moves the agent further from the goal. The authors name this inversion phenomenon a "Mirage."

This audit reveals three key facts. First, in official released JEPA-WM weights, the top-ranked action is suboptimal in over 96.8% of Push-T anchors and virtually 100% of MetaWorld anchors, showing severe structural Mirages. Second, neither increasing candidate sampling budgets (via CEM) nor upgrading backbones to powerful V-JEPA 1/2 encoders fixes the defect. Third, this critical flaw remained hidden until now because step-by-step closed-loop replanning was constantly scrubbing away errors in real time.

sections.heading: Value-Driven Models, Geometric Corrections, and the Role of This Audit
sections.summary: Unlike value-driven models like Dreamer or TD-MPC, JEPA-style architectures rely on latent distance itself as an evaluator. While prior works cited geometric distortions as motivation for workarounds, none quantitatively benchmarked released models as evaluators.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Two Lineages of Latent World Models
Latent world models broadly divide into two families based on how they score futures. "Value-driven" models, such as Dreamer and TD-MPC, evaluate simulated rollouts in latent space using learned reward functions or value heads. Here, evaluator quality has long been studied in terms of value estimation error. In contrast, "reward-free" models like JEPA-WM discard value heads and use Euclidean distance within a frozen latent space directly as the planning objective. Consequently, existing diagnostic tools developed for value functions cannot be applied directly.

### 2.2 Geometric Concerns: From Motivation to Measurement
Past research (e.g., trajectory straightening) has highlighted that self-supervised feature spaces are curved—making Euclidean distance a poor proxy for progress—and that inverse dynamics models assume smooth spaces. However, these points were only treated as motivation to pitch new methods. Nobody had built a benchmark to measure how frequently and severely official released JEPA-WM evaluation objectives actually fail.

### 2.3 What Surrounding Mitigations and Adaptive Replanners Concealed
Recently, numerous techniques around closed-loop planning have emerged, such as goal-conditioned inverse dynamics models (GC-IDM) to amortize planning, AdaReP to adapt replanning frequency based on divergence, and AdaJEPA to update latent models at test time. However, none of these measure the intrinsic action-rankability of the frozen latent space. ARC-Bench provides this direct measurement and clarifies why high-frequency replanning served as a cover for these flaws.

sections.heading: The ARC-Bench Protocol: Auditing Evaluators with Zero Leakage
sections.summary: ARC-Bench isolates pure ranking ability using fixed candidate action sets and ground-truth costs. Localization probes further verify that task-relevant information is present in the representations, but unexploited by the frozen latent objective.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation and Metrics
The basic unit of audit is an "anchor." An anchor consists of context observations, a goal, and a fixed set of $C$ candidate action sequences. Each candidate is assigned an offline "ground-truth cost" calculated as the geometric distance between the actual (or simulated) reached terminal state and the goal terminal state (which the planner never sees at test time).
Reported metrics include "top-1 regret" (difference in true cost between the top-1 chosen candidate and the optimal candidate), Hit@1 and Hit@3, Spearman rank correlation, wrong-anchor rate (the percentage of anchors where top-1 is not optimal), and strong-Mirage rate (where a candidate in the worse half of true costs ends up in the top quartile of top-1 regret).

### 3.2 A Strict, No-Leak Protocol
Model selection is conducted exclusively on validation splits, with testing run once on fully held-out splits (256 anchors $\times$ 12 candidates each in maze domains). The audit pipeline guards against hyperparameter tuning and threshold leakage, verifying full reproducibility across three seeds.

### 3.3 Backbones and Testbeds
The benchmark adopts four environments: navigation domains "PointMaze" and "Wall", alongside manipulation domains "Push-T" and "MetaWorld reach-wall". The PointMaze checkpoint matches the SHA-256 hash in the official repository byte-for-byte, ruling out local training bugs. Furthermore, controlled experiments isolate visual backbone effects by swapping DINOv2 with V-JEPA 1 (ViT-L) and V-JEPA 2 (ViT-L, ViT-G) in Push-T and MetaWorld.

### 3.4 Localization Probes and Circularity Controls
To address whether the action evaluation information was missing from the setup altogether, the authors trained lightweight second-stage probes (Extremely Randomized Trees and k-NN) to predict terminal displacement from actions and rank them. Even when these probes had high terminal prediction error, ranking improved substantially. This localization proves that the necessary ranking information is present, but the frozen latent objective fails to extract it.

sections.heading: Fixed-Candidate Audits: Action Ranking Is Structurally Broken
sections.summary: Official JEPA-WM checkpoints pick suboptimal actions as top-1 in 96.8% of Push-T and 100% of MetaWorld anchors. Neither switching to video-pretrained encoders (V-JEPA) nor testing pure topology stress in mazes fixes this inversion.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Official Objectives Invert Action Order Across Domains
Auditing candidate actions with official checkpoints yields disastrous results. In Push-T (5 seeds, 618 valid anchors), the wrong-anchor rate of the official L2 planning objective reaches 96.8%, with Hit@1 at only 3.2% and an average top-1 regret of 0.243.
MetaWorld reach-wall (750 valid anchors) is even worse: wrong-anchor rate is 100.0% and Hit@1 is 0.0%. Furthermore, rank correlation between predicted scores and true costs is strongly negative, showing an outright inversion where actions scored as better by the model are actually worse. In PointMaze, 24.2% of anchors exhibit severe Mirages.

### 4.2 Video-Pretrained Backbones Do Not Heal Ranking Deficits
The authors tested the hypothesis that video-pretrained V-JEPA models might capture action dynamics better than static image encoders like DINOv2. The results were negative. In Push-T, across all V-JEPA 1 and 2 scales, wrong-anchor rates remain between 91.1% and 97.3%. In MetaWorld, Hit@1 and Hit@3 stay at 0% across all backbones. The latent objective consistently favors unhelpful action families (random, periodic, or stationary motion) over direct progress toward the goal.

### 4.3 Controlled Topology Stress Audits
To confirm that this issue stems from the geometry of terminal Euclidean distance rather than undertrained weights, the authors conducted coordinate-based topology audits on U-Maze and MiniGrid/FourRooms. When obstacles force detours, terminal Euclidean distance misranks the top candidate in 100% of anchors (Hit@1 = 0%), and Manhattan distance provides no meaningful fix. Minimizing straight-line distance in environments with obstacles is the structural root cause of ranking breakdown.

captions.F1: Audit results using the official JEPA-WM objective. In Push-T and MetaWorld reach-wall, wrong-anchor rates approach 100% (left) and generate large top-1 regret (right).
captions.F2: Qualitative rollouts from encoder-swap audits. For each panel, the top row shows the action chosen by the frozen latent objective, and the bottom row shows the true optimal action. Even when the selected motions look plausible, they fail to make progress toward the goal.
captions.F3: Topology stress diagnostics on U-Maze and MiniGrid/FourRooms. Even with pure geometric terminal distance without learned models, obstacle topologies cause incorrect action choices 100% of the time.

sections.heading: Why It Stayed Hidden: How Closed-Loop Replanning Masks the Flaw
sections.summary: Increasing sampling budgets does not change the relative ranking among evaluators. However, widening the replanning interval from 1 to 6 steps collapses success rates, proving that frequent replanning was continuously masking single-step evaluation errors.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Increasing Candidate Budgets Does Not Fix Action Ordering
One might wonder if planners like CEM overcome this by sampling many candidates to find elites. Audits varying candidate budgets $B \in \{2, 4, 8, 12\}$ show that while higher budgets improve the best candidate found overall, the relative performance ranking between evaluators remains identical. If an evaluator ranks actions by a flawed criterion, sampling more candidates cannot solve the fundamental issue.

### 5.2 The Gap Between Single-Step Scoring and Closed-Loop Control
The authors also tried inserting the lightweight probe from Section 3 directly into the CEM loop. However, the probe's correlation vanished on the out-of-distribution actions generated online, failing to improve closed-loop planning. Patching only the scoring function cannot effortlessly cross the closed-loop barrier.

### 5.3 Closed-Loop Replanning Masks Broken Action Ranking
How, then, did official models solve tasks? The answer is step-by-step replanning ($k=1$). By receiving fresh observations and re-anchoring the latent state every single step, a poor action choice at one step is corrected in the next before mistakes can accumulate.
To prove this, the authors varied the replanning interval $k$ from $k=1$ (every step) to $k=6$ (every 6 steps). The effect was immediate. In PointMaze, success dropped by 27.8 points from 89.6% to 61.8% ($p=1.51 \times 10^{-9}$). In Push-T, success plummeted by 23.6 points from 36.1% to 12.5% ($p=1.08 \times 10^{-9}$).
Furthermore, analyzing the initial plan in PointMaze showed that 41.7% of episodes rescued by step-by-step replanning were episodes that suffered severe Mirages on their very first plan. High-frequency replanning did not provide true robustness; it merely reset broken evaluator mistakes behind the scenes.

captions.F4: Regret trends across varying CEM-style candidate budgets $B$. While increasing sample counts improves overall candidate quality, the relative performance ordering between evaluators remains unchanged, showing sampling cannot compensate for evaluator flaws.
captions.F5: Collapse of closed-loop success as replanning interval $k$ widens. In both PointMaze (navigation) and Push-T (manipulation), moving from $k=1$ to $k=6$ severely reduces success rates, demonstrating statistically that frequent replanning masked underlying defects.
captions.F6: Replanning interval comparisons across models including video backbones (V-JEPA). In Push-T, extending the open-loop window to $k=6$ drastically reduces success across all backbones, confirming the same masking phenomenon.

sections.heading: Discussion: Success Rates Do Not Guarantee Good Representations
sections.summary: Equating high closed-loop success rates with good representations conflates control loop error suppression with representation quality. Because this flaw leads directly to failure in settings where replanning is expensive, single-step ranking audits are essential.
sections.details:
### Success Rates Overstate Representation Quality
Prior research has treated closed-loop planning success as evidence that frozen latent spaces are well-suited for planning. This work shows that such success conflates two entirely separate factors: the representation's action-ranking ability, and the control loop's capacity to suppress errors. Switching to video backbones does not cure this latent distance defect. Future research on reward-free world models should report single-step action-ranking metrics (like ARC-Bench) alongside closed-loop success, and explicitly state replanning frequencies and computational costs.

### The True Nature of Recent Mitigations
Recent methods like amortizing planning with inverse dynamics (GC-IDM), adapting replanning frequencies (AdaReP), and test-time model adaptation (AdaJEPA) can be viewed as implicit coping mechanisms for an unspoken flaw: latent distance cannot be trusted. ARC-Bench turns this unstated problem into concrete, measurable numbers.

### Practical Implications for Applications
In domains where replanning is computationally cheap and high-frequency observations are readily available, this defect can be tolerated by paying an extra computational cost ($k=1$ uses up to $6\times$ more planner queries than $k=6$). However, in robotics systems where replanning is slow, where observations are intermittent, or in real-world tasks where a single wrong action is irreversible, this flaw triggers immediate, catastrophic failure.

sections.heading: Limitations of This Study
sections.summary: This paper focuses on diagnosing the flaw and explaining its mechanism rather than proposing an all-in-one replacement planner. Some analyses also rely on specific environments or released checkpoints.
sections.details:
The authors note the following limitations:
- The localization probe in Section 3 is strictly a diagnostic tool to verify that information exists, not a full-fledged planning method. As shown in Section 5.2, plugging the probe directly into closed-loop execution does not work out of the box.
- Audits on official Push-T and MetaWorld checkpoints score pre-generated candidates rather than running a complete end-to-end CEM iterative search from scratch.
- V-JEPA backbone experiments are controlled comparisons on Push-T and MetaWorld reach-wall, and do not span every existing video JEPA planner or domain.
- The diagnostic linking initial-plan Mirage severity to closed-loop rescue rates is currently established specifically in PointMaze.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Start by Questioning the Evaluation Objective
sections.summary: The implicit assumption that latent distance reliably ranks actions fails structurally even in official JEPA-WM checkpoints. Rather than relying solely on closed-loop success rates, auditing evaluators directly with ARC-Bench will be essential for future progress.
sections.details:
Reward-free latent world models have relied on the intuitive assumption that closeness in latent space reflects action quality. However, rigorous audits via ARC-Bench demonstrate that this assumption fails structurally and severely in official checkpoints.

This breakdown is not fixed by increasing sampling budgets or switching to video-pretrained encoders. The fatal defect stayed hidden until now only because step-by-step closed-loop replanning rapidly overwrote errors at every turn.

Assuming a representation is sound just because closed-loop execution works is risky. To properly evaluate planner scoring objectives and develop truly robust latent representations, adopting objective audit protocols like ARC-Bench will be vital for future robotics and world model research.

sections.heading: Appendix: Details for Full Reproducibility
sections.summary: This section summarizes key experimental configurations, including fixed-candidate pool construction, official action chunk formats, and CEM planner parameters.
sections.details:
### Candidate Action Pools and Audit Data
For maze domains, the fixed-candidate audit uses isolated test sets of 256 anchors per domain, each containing 12 candidate action sequences. For Push-T and MetaWorld, the setup follows official JEPA-WM evaluation code using action chunks (6 steps $\times$ 10 dims for Push-T, 6 steps $\times$ 20 dims for MetaWorld) across 750 anchors with 32 candidate rollouts.

### Closed-Loop Planning Setup
In closed-loop masking experiments, PointMaze uses the official configuration with gym 0.23.1 and mujoco-py, while Push-T follows the official JEPA-WM online evaluation pipeline. The only manipulated parameter is the replanning interval $k \in \{1, 2, 4, 6\}$. Planner hyperparameters are fixed to a horizon of 6, 5 CEM iterations, 64 samples, and 8 elites. For encoder-swap experiments, evaluations use 128 samples, 16 elites, and 10 iterations.

takeaways: High task success rates do not guarantee that a world model's latent representation is good; high-frequency replanning (MPC) can mask a fundamentally broken evaluator.
Euclidean distance in frozen latent spaces easily inverts true task costs (creating Mirages) in environments with obstacles or non-linear dynamics.
Upgrading to powerful video-pretrained features (V-JEPA) does not resolve broken action ranking as long as simple terminal latent distance is used as the objective.
When developing or evaluating latent planning models, researchers should audit single-step action ranking (Hit@1 and regret) directly and stress-test systems by reducing replanning frequency.
limitations: While the paper clearly demonstrates ranking failures on fixed candidates, it does not propose a universal plug-and-play replacement evaluator that works directly in closed-loop settings.
Audits of official manipulation checkpoints (Push-T, MetaWorld) evaluate scoring on candidate sets rather than full iterative CEM search reruns.
The correlation between initial-plan Mirage severity and replanning rescue rates is currently detailed and proven specifically in the PointMaze domain.
